text:
**Short answer:** A 1,000 Wh station with a surge rating of at least about 1,300 W can keep a typical full-size fridge running most of a day. For a full 24 hours, plan for roughly 1,600 to 2,000 Wh, and for two days, about 2,800 Wh.

**The three things to check**

1. **Continuous output (watts):** The fridge's running draw is usually 100 to 250 W, so almost any 1,000 Wh-class station handles it. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))
2. **Surge (startup) output:** This is the number that most often blocks a fridge. The compressor spikes to roughly 1,200 to 2,400 W when it starts, and if the station's surge rating is lower, its protection trips at startup. Sources use a 1,200 W to 1,300 W allowance for a typical fridge ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/); [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). Larger or older fridges can need 2,400 W or more, so a margin is wise. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))
3. **Watt-hours (capacity):** A fridge's compressor runs only about 30 to 40% of the time, so its average draw is much lower than its running watts. A typical full-size fridge averages about 41 W over a day, or about 1,000 Wh per day before losses and about 1,400 Wh with inverter losses and headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

**Quick sizing by outage length** (typical fridge, using the 1,400 Wh/day figure above)

| Outage | Battery needed |
|---|---|
| ~12 hours | ~700 Wh or more |
| 1 day | ~1,400 Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800 Wh |

**Find your fridge's real number:** Check the yellow EnergyGuide label for annual kWh. Divide kWh per year × 1,000 by 8,760 to get average watts. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about twice the typical figure, and a small apartment fridge about half ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). The U.S. Department of Energy's [Refrigerator and Freezer Energy Rating Search Tool](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/) can also give model-specific estimates.

**Examples from the guides**

- **BLUETTI AC180:** 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W AC, 2,700 W peak, pure sine wave. BlackBox calls it a top pick for a fridge. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2:** 1,070 Wh, estimated at about 17 hours for a fridge in HomeGridHQ's model. ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/))
- **Anker SOLIX S2000:** 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W rated AC, 3,000 W peak, pure sine wave. It's a 2 kWh-class option for longer outages. ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator))

I don't have verified store links for these, so please check current prices and availability on the guide pages above. Runtimes are estimates, and they vary by fridge and conditions.

**Tips for outages**

- Keep the fridge door shut. The USDA says food is unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Choose a pure sine wave inverter. Cheap modified-sine units can make compressor motors run hot or fail to start ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).
- Compact power stations under about 300 Wh are usually too small for a fridge, because their surge output falls below the startup allowance ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
